title: Text invitations can speed survey response, but access and consent differ across groups
source_unit: Census Research Report Series methodology paper using Census Household Panel paradata and survey responses from the May 2024 topical
geography: United States; nationally representative Census Household Panel members and approximately 10,000 May 2024 topical respondents

observations.period: May 2024 Census Household Panel topical; paper published September 2026

denominator.unit: approximately 10,000 topical respondents; study-specific consent and access denominators vary

response_timing.value: text invitations appeared to bolster initial response in the hours immediately after receipt

text_access.value: propensity to access the survey through text differed by age, race/ethnicity, education, family income, and respondent type

consent.value: text-message consent was approximately 50%, comparable to existing literature

consent_differences.value: consent behavior differed by race/ethnicity, age, family income, education, marital status, region, and respondent type

observations.method: The paper analyzes paradata and survey responses from a probability-based longitudinal Census Household Panel, comparing text and email invitation behavior and modeling text-message consent and access patterns.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census methodology working paper, not a Census Bureau policy endorsement. The result concerns survey contact and response behavior, not political participation or general digital access; the topical, consent, and access universes differ and the abstract does not establish why each person consented or responded.
observations.subgroup: Census Household Panel members and May 2024 topical respondents, separated by demographic and respondent-type characteristics reported in the study.
observations.counterinterpretation: Text can lower contact time and cost for some people while creating privacy, device, language, disability, or message-trust barriers for others. Faster response may improve data collection without proving lower burden, representative participation, or greater trust in government.

related_sources.claim: A separate Census evaluation documents longer-run changes in ACS self-response contact strategies; it is related institutional context, not the same panel or text-consent estimate.

boundary: This record adds a digital-contact-to-institutional-response pathway. It does not establish household trust, equal burden, population representativeness, political participation, policy responsiveness, or a same-person route from message receipt to later civic outcome.
